hints: Think about what must stay exactly the same for two compounds to be isomers, count the atoms of each element.
Think about what must be different in how those same atoms are joined together or arranged.
walkthrough:
Fix what is the same**
Picture building two models using exactly the same set of atoms, for example five carbons and ten hydrogens. If the molecular formula $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}$ is identical, you have the first condition for isomerism.

Spot what is different**
Now join those same atoms in a different order. In Fig. 4.1 both $\text{P}$ and $\text{Q}$ are $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}$ alkenes, but the double bond is in a different position and the carbon skeleton branches differently. Same atoms, different connectivity means structural isomers.

Final answer: Compounds with the same molecular formula / same number of atoms of each element
but with different structural formulae / different structures.

hints: Look at $\text{P}$, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_3$, and notice each $\text{C}$ of the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ carries two different groups.
Recall why the two groups cannot swap sides without breaking the pi bond.
walkthrough:
Read the structure of P**
$\text{P}$ is pent-2-ene, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_3$. On the left $\text{C}$ of the double bond you have $\text{H}$ and $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, on the right $\text{C}$ you have $\text{H}$ and $\text{CH}_3$. In the diagram both alkyl groups are on the same side, so this is cis-pent-2-ene.

Draw the opposite geometry**
To get the other geometrical isomer, keep all the connectivity the same but place the two alkyl groups on opposite sides of the double bond. That gives trans-pent-2-ene, with $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2$ up on one carbon and $\text{CH}_3$ down on the other, or vice versa.

Explain why they stay different**
A $\text{C}=\text{C}$ bond contains a pi bond formed by sideways overlap of p orbitals. Twisting one end would break that overlap, so rotation is locked. Because the groups cannot rotate past each other, cis and trans forms cannot interconvert and remain distinct, non identical isomers.

Final answer: Draw of trans-pent-2-ene: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_3$ with $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2$ and $\text{CH}_3$ on opposite sides of $\text{C}=\text{C}$ (P is the cis form).
There is restricted / no rotation about the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond, so the two spatial arrangements are locked and are not identical.

hints: Focus on the electron rich $\text{C}=\text{C}$ bond attacking an electrophile derived from $\text{Br}_2$.
walkthrough:
Link the reagents to the pathway**
Alkenes are electron rich at the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ bond because of the exposed pi electrons. $\text{Br}_2$ is polarised to $\text{Br}^{\delta+}$ on approach, so the pi bond donates to the electrophile $\text{Br}^+$. Addition across the double bond initiated by an electrophile is electrophilic addition.

hints: Write out $\text{Q}$ as $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{CHCH}_3$ and mark where the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ bond will split.
Remember that a $\text{C}$ with two alkyl groups gives a ketone, while a $\text{C}$ with one alkyl group and one $\text{H}$ gives a carboxylic acid under vigorous oxidation.
walkthrough:
Split the double bond**
$\text{Q}$ is 2-methylbut-2-ene, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{CHCH}_3$. Hot concentrated acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$ cleaves the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ completely. Think of cutting between the two doubly bonded carbons and adding $\text{O}$ atoms to each fragment.

Assign each fragment**
The left carbon $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=$ has two methyl groups and no $\text{H}$, so it becomes the ketone propanone, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$. The right carbon $=\text{CHCH}_3$ has one $\text{H}$, so vigorous oxidation takes it all the way to ethanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$. Balancing $\text{O}$ atoms with $[\text{O}]$ gives $$(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{CHCH}_3 + 3[\text{O}] \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3 + \text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$$

Final answer: Products are $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3 + \text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$
$$(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{CHCH}_3 + 3[\text{O}] \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3 + \text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$$

hints: Compare the two possible carbocations formed when $\text{H}^+$ adds to either end of the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ in $\text{Q}$.
Think about how alkyl groups push electron density toward a positive carbon and stabilise it.
walkthrough:
See the two routes**
When $\text{HBr}$ adds, $\text{H}^+$ adds first to make a carbocation, then $\text{Br}^-$ attacks. Adding $\text{H}^+$ to one end of $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{CHCH}_3$ gives a tertiary carbocation $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}^+\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, adding to the other end gives a secondary carbocation $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}^+\text{CH}_3$. Product $\text{S}$ comes from the tertiary ion, $\text{R}$ from the secondary ion.

Rank the intermediates**
Alkyl groups release electron density by the positive inductive effect, spreading and stabilising the positive charge. The tertiary carbocation has three alkyl groups around $\text{C}^+$, the secondary has only two. The more stabilised tertiary intermediate forms faster and in greater amount, so $\text{S}$ is the major product.

Final answer: S is formed via the more stable carbocation intermediate.
This is because of the greater positive inductive effect from more alkyl groups attached to the positively charged carbon.

hints: Calculate the $M_r$ of $\text{R}$, $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{11}\text{Br}$, using $79$ and $81$ for bromine to see why two peaks appear.
Recall that the molecular ion is the whole molecule with one electron removed, shown in brackets with the charge outside.
walkthrough:
Check the masses**
$\text{R}$ is $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{11}\text{Br}$. With $^{79}\text{Br}$: $5(12)+11(1)+79 = 150$. With $^{81}\text{Br}$: $5(12)+11(1)+81 = 152$. Bromine exists as roughly equal $^{79}\text{Br}$ and $^{81}\text{Br}$ isotopes, so the molecular ion appears as a pair two units apart.

Draw the ions correctly**
Remove one electron from the whole $\text{R}$ molecule to give the molecular ion. Draw the full carbon skeleton of $\text{R}$ with $\text{Br}$, put square brackets around it, write $^{79}\text{Br}$ for the $m/e = 150$ ion and $^{81}\text{Br}$ for the $m/e = 152$ ion, with $+$ outside the bracket: $[\text{C}_5\text{H}_{11}{}^{79}\text{Br}]^+$ and $[\text{C}_5\text{H}_{11}{}^{81}\text{Br}]^+$.

Final answer: peak at $m/e = 150$: $[\text{C}_5\text{H}_{11}{}^{79}\text{Br}]^+$ with $^{79}\text{Br}$ and + outside brackets
peak at $m/e = 152$: $[\text{C}_5\text{H}_{11}{}^{81}\text{Br}]^+$ with $^{81}\text{Br}$ and + outside brackets
(structural formula of R with Br shown, e.g. $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}(\text{Br})\text{CH}_3$ as the ion skeleton)

hints: Note that $\text{Br}$ in $\text{T}$ is replaced by $\text{CN}$ in $\text{U}$, and recall which solvent favours substitution over elimination.
walkthrough:
Choose the cyanide source**
Changing $\text{R-Br}$ to $\text{R-CN}$ is nucleophilic substitution by $\text{CN}^-$. Supply it as $\text{KCN}$ (or $\text{NaCN}$) dissolved in ethanol with heating. Ethanol is key because aqueous conditions would favour substitution to an alcohol, while ethanolic conditions deliver the nitrile cleanly.
Final answer: $\text{KCN}$ in ethanol, heat

hints: Remember acid hydrolysis of $\text{RCN}$ needs water plus $\text{HCl}$ and gives $\text{RCOOH}$ plus $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$.
walkthrough:
Build the hydrolysis equation**
The nitrile carbon becomes the carboxyl carbon. $\text{U}$ is $(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2\text{CHCN}$. Add $2\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to supply $\text{O}$ and $\text{H}$, with $\text{HCl(aq)}$ providing acid conditions. The organic product is $\text{V}$, $(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2\text{CHCOOH}$, and nitrogen ends up as $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$: $$(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2\text{CHCN} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{HCl} \rightarrow (\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2\text{CHCOOH} + \text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$$

hints: Identify the reaction between a carboxylic acid $\text{V}$ and an alcohol with concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ catalyst.
Name the functional group formed when $\text{COOH} + \text{OH}$ lose water.
Add the carbons of $\text{V}$ ($\text{C}_6$) and propan-2-ol ($\text{C}_3$) and subtract $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ lost.
walkthrough:
Name the reaction type**
Carboxylic acid $\text{V}$, $(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2\text{CHCOOH}$, plus propan-2-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_3$, with a catalytic amount of $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is the classic esterification. Two molecules join with loss of water, so it is also classified as condensation.

Name the functional group**
$\text{RCOOH} + \text{R'OH} \rightarrow \text{RCOOR'} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. The $\text{COOH}$ group is converted into $\text{COOR'}$, which is an ester linkage.

Work out the formula of W**
$\text{V}$ is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_2$ and propan-2-ol is $\text{C}_3\text{H}_8\text{O}$. Combine and subtract $\text{H}_2\text{O}$: $\text{C}_{6+3} = \text{C}_9$, $\text{H}_{12+8-2} = \text{H}_{18}$, $\text{O}_{2+1-1} = \text{O}_2$. So $\text{W}$ is $\text{C}_9\text{H}_{18}\text{O}_2$.

Final answer: type of reaction: condensation / esterification
functional group formed: ester
molecular formula of W: $\text{C}_9\text{H}_{18}\text{O}_2$
